title: Data visualisation with matplotlib
summary: Turn numbers into clear charts with matplotlib — line, scatter, bar and histogram plots you can label, style and save.
objectives: Create a figure and axes with plt.subplots and understand the object model
Draw line, scatter, bar and histogram plots from lists or arrays
Label axes, add a title and a legend so a chart explains itself
Plot pandas Series and DataFrame columns directly
Control style, colour, markers and figure size
Save a chart to a file with savefig for reports and notebooks

quiz.q: Which call creates a figure and a single axes you can draw on?
quiz.why: fig, ax = plt.subplots() returns a Figure and an Axes; you call methods like ax.plot on the axes.

quiz.q: Which plot type best shows the distribution of a single numeric column?
quiz.why: A histogram buckets values into bins and shows how frequently each range occurs — ideal for one variable's distribution.

quiz.q: What is the standard import alias for matplotlib's plotting interface?
options: from matplotlib import plot as plt
quiz.why: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt is the universal convention; plt gives you the plotting functions.

quiz.q: Which method shows a label that explains each line in the chart, using the label= text you passed to plot?
quiz.why: After giving each plot a label=, calling ax.legend() draws the key (legend) that maps colours to labels.

quiz.q: Which method writes the current chart to a PNG file?
quiz.why: fig.savefig("chart.png") saves the figure to disk; do it before plt.show() in scripts so the figure still exists.

quiz.q: Why is the 'object-oriented' style (fig, ax) preferred over the pyplot state machine?
quiz.answer: It is explicit about which axes you are drawing on, so it scales to multiple subplots and is easier to read.
quiz.why: The state-machine style (plt.plot, plt.title) hides which axes is 'current'; fig, ax makes every call unambiguous.

body_markdown:
## Why visualise data?

Numbers in a table hide their shape. A **chart** lets you see a trend, an outlier, or a distribution in a single glance. As a maths graduate you already think in functions and distributions — matplotlib lets you *draw* them.

**matplotlib** is the foundational plotting library in Python. pandas, seaborn and many others build on top of it, so learning it pays off everywhere.

## The figure and axes model

Every chart lives on a **Figure** (the whole canvas) which holds one or more **Axes** (a single plot with its x and y). The clean, modern way is to create both at once, then call methods on the axes.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("x squared")
ax.set_title("A simple line")
plt.show()
```

Prefer this `fig, ax` style over bare `plt.plot(...)`. It is explicit about *which* plot you are drawing on, which matters the moment you have more than one.

## The common plot types

Four plots cover most early needs:

- `ax.plot(x, y)` — a **line**, good for trends over time.
- `ax.scatter(x, y)` — **points**, good for relationships between two variables.
- `ax.bar(labels, values)` — **bars**, good for comparing categories.
- `ax.hist(values, bins=20)` — a **histogram**, good for one variable's distribution.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]
sales = [120, 150, 130]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(months, sales, color="steelblue")
ax.set_title("Sales by month")
ax.set_ylabel("Units")
plt.show()
```

## Labelling and legends

An unlabelled chart is a puzzle. Always add axis labels and a title. When you draw several series, give each a `label=` and call `ax.legend()` to show the key.

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], label="linear")
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], label="quadratic")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

## Plotting with pandas

In practice your data lives in a **DataFrame**. pandas wraps matplotlib, so `df.plot()` works, but you can also pass columns straight to an axes for full control.

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.DataFrame({"day": [1, 2, 3], "temp": [14, 16, 15]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(df["day"], df["temp"], marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.set_ylabel("Temp (C)")
plt.show()
```

## Saving your work

In a notebook a chart just appears. In a script, call `fig.savefig` to write a file — do this **before** `plt.show()` so the figure still exists.

```python
fig.savefig("temperature.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

## Your task

Load a small CSV with pandas and make **two** charts from it — one line or scatter, one bar or histogram — fully labelled, and save each as a PNG.

slides.narration: Welcome back. So far this month you've loaded and reshaped data with pandas. Now it's time to see it. In this lesson we'll cover matplotlib, the foundational plotting library in Python. By the end you'll be able to turn a column of numbers into a clear, labelled chart, choose the right plot type, and save it to a file for your reports.

slides.title: Why visualise data?
bullets: A table of numbers hides its shape.
A chart shows trends, outliers, distributions.
matplotlib underpins pandas and seaborn.
You already think in functions and distributions.
slides.narration: Why bother plotting at all? Because a wall of numbers hides what's really going on. A single chart can reveal a trend, an outlier, or the shape of a distribution in one glance. matplotlib is the library nearly everything else builds on, including pandas and seaborn, so the time you invest here pays off across all your tools. As a maths graduate, you already think in functions and distributions. Now you'll draw them.

slides.title: Figure and axes
bullets: A Figure is the whole canvas.
An Axes is one plot, with x and y.
plt.subplots gives you both at once.
Then call methods on the axes.
slides.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
slides.narration: Matplotlib has two key objects. The Figure is the whole canvas, and an Axes is a single plot living on it, with its own x and y. The clean way to start is plt dot subplots, which hands you both a figure and an axes. From then on you draw by calling methods on that axes object, like ax dot plot. This is called the object-oriented style.

slides.title: The standard import
bullets: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt.
plt is the universal alias.
plt.show displays the window or output.
In notebooks the chart just appears.
slides.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
# ... draw on ax ...
plt.show()
slides.narration: Almost every matplotlib script starts the same way: import matplotlib dot pyplot as p l t. That alias, p l t, is a universal convention, so stick to it. When you're done drawing, plt dot show pops up the window in a script, or renders the chart inline in a notebook. Get into the habit of these two lines as your bookends.

slides.title: Line and scatter plots
bullets: ax.plot for trends and time series.
ax.scatter for relationships between two variables.
Add markers to highlight data points.
slides.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y, marker="o", label="trend")
ax.scatter(x, y2, color="red")
plt.show()
slides.narration: The two most common plots are line and scatter. Use ax dot plot when you have a trend or a time series, where points are connected in order. Use ax dot scatter when you want to see the relationship between two variables, with each observation as its own dot. You can add markers to a line plot too, so individual data points stand out.

slides.title: Bars and histograms
bullets: ax.bar compares categories.
ax.hist shows one variable's distribution.
bins controls how finely a histogram buckets.
Choose the plot that fits the question.
slides.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Jan", "Feb"], [120, 150])
# or:
ax.hist(values, bins=20)
plt.show()
slides.narration: For categories, reach for a bar chart with ax dot bar, comparing values across labels like months. For the distribution of a single numeric column, use a histogram with ax dot hist, which buckets values into bins and shows how often each range occurs. The bins argument controls how fine those buckets are. Always pick the plot that matches the question you're asking.

slides.title: Label everything
bullets: set_xlabel, set_ylabel, set_title.
An unlabelled chart is a puzzle.
Give each series a label= and call ax.legend().
A good chart explains itself.
slides.narration: A chart with no labels is a puzzle nobody wants to solve. Always set an x label, a y label, and a title, using set underscore x label, set underscore y label, and set underscore title. When you draw more than one line, give each one a label argument, then call ax dot legend to show the key that maps colours to names. A good chart explains itself without you in the room.

slides.title: Plotting with pandas
bullets: Your data usually lives in a DataFrame.
df.plot() works as a quick shortcut.
Or pass columns to an axes for control.
matplotlib runs underneath pandas.
slides.code:
import pandas as pd
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(df["day"], df["temp"], marker="o")
plt.show()
slides.narration: In real work your data sits in a pandas DataFrame. pandas is built on top of matplotlib, so the quick shortcut df dot plot just works. But for full control, create your figure and axes and pass the columns straight in, like ax dot plot of df day and df temp. This gives you all of matplotlib's styling while keeping pandas for the data handling.

slides.title: Style and size
bullets: color, marker, linestyle change appearance.
figsize sets the figure dimensions.
Keep it clean: clarity over decoration.
slides.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(x, y, color="steelblue",
        linestyle="--", marker="o")
plt.show()
slides.narration: You can control how a chart looks. Color sets the colour, marker chooses the point shape, and linestyle changes solid to dashed. To make the whole figure bigger or wider, pass figsize to plt dot subplots as a width and height in inches. A word of advice though: aim for clarity, not decoration. The goal is a chart that's easy to read, not a fireworks display.

slides.title: Saving charts
bullets: fig.savefig writes a PNG or PDF.
Save before plt.show() in a script.
dpi controls resolution, bbox_inches trims edges.
slides.narration: In a notebook the chart appears on its own, but in a script you'll want to keep it. Call fig dot savefig with a filename to write a P N G or P D F to disk. One gotcha: save before you call plt dot show in a script, because show can clear the figure. The d p i argument sets resolution, and bounding box inches set to tight trims off the white border.

plot, scatter, bar, hist cover most needs.
Label axes, title, and legend every time.

Always label your axes, add a title, and a legend when you have multiple series. And save your work with fig dot savefig.
